title: Plans to go out, with the near future

tips.title: Aller + infinitive is the whole tense
tips.body: The near future is **the present tense of aller** followed by **an infinitive**: *je vais sortir, on va manger, ils vont regarder un film*. Nothing else changes. If *aller* is right and the second verb is in the dictionary form, the tense is right.

tips.title: Aller is irregular
tips.body: *Je **vais**, tu **vas**, il **va**, nous **allons**, vous **allez**, ils **vont**.* Four of the six forms do not look like *aller* at all. This one verb is now doing all the work, so it has to be automatic.

tips.title: The negative wraps aller, not the infinitive
tips.body: *Je **ne vais pas** sortir* — *ne … pas* goes round the conjugated verb, *aller*. *Je vais ne pas sortir* is wrong every time.

tips.title: Time markers announce the tense
tips.body: *Ce soir, demain, ce week-end, samedi prochain, la semaine prochaine, pendant les vacances.* Start the sentence with one and the examiner knows a future is coming before *aller* appears — and so do you.

tips.title: Invite with on va, accept with je veux bien
tips.body: *On va au cinéma ce soir ?* — *Oui, je veux bien !* / *Désolé, je ne peux pas, je dois faire mes devoirs.* Three lines cover an invitation, an acceptance and a refusal with a reason, and they are exactly what a conversation or a writing task about going out needs.

why.matters: The near future is the first tense after the present, and it is the cheapest range you will ever add: the present of *aller* plus an infinitive, *je vais sortir*, exactly as English says *I am going to go out*. It exists so that a paragraph can point forward, which the mark scheme counts as a second time frame. The topic wraps it in the French of making plans: inviting someone, accepting, refusing politely with *je dois*, naming a time and a place, and reading a time in the 24-hour clock that French uses without thinking.

examples.title: The group chat on Friday
examples.body: A plan for Saturday is a sentence in the near future and a question: *On va manger une pizza, tu veux venir ?* Every message in the thread is the same grammar. The only verb that changes is *aller*, in its six irregular forms; the second verb never moves, so *going to go* is *aller aller* with no embarrassment. Add a time, a place and a *ça va être génial*, and you have the exam's picture task in a text message.

visual.alt: A conjugation table of aller in the present, all six forms irregular, the verb that builds the near future with an infinitive after it

examples.title: Refusing without offence
examples.body: An invitation needs an answer, and French has set phrases for each. *Tu veux venir ?* is answered with *oui, je veux bien* or *d'accord*, and a refusal comes with an excuse built on *je dois*: *désolé, je ne peux pas, je dois faire mes devoirs*. Conversations and writing tasks about going out ask for exactly this kind of exchange, and the three verbs behind it, *vouloir, pouvoir, devoir*, take an infinitive every time, so one conjugated verb carries the whole reply.

examples.title: Reading dix-neuf heures trente
examples.body: A French cinema listing says *19h30*, and a French friend says *dix-neuf heures trente*. Neither means anything until you subtract twelve: it is 7:30 pm. Timetables, station boards and invitations all use the 24-hour clock, and the listening paper reads times out in it, so *à sept heures et demie* and *à dix-neuf heures trente* are the same moment said two ways. Practise both until the subtraction is automatic, because a wrong time is a missed film.

steps.title: Le futur proche
steps.body:
To say what you are **going to do**, French does what English does: the verb *to go* plus the verb you mean.

**Aller** (present tense) **+ infinitive**:

*Je **vais** sortir* — I am going to go out. *On **va** manger une pizza* — we are going to eat a pizza. *Ils **vont** regarder un film* — they are going to watch a film.

**Aller** is irregular: *je vais, tu vas, il/elle/on va, nous allons, vous allez, ils/elles vont*.

The second verb **never changes** — it is the infinitive: *sortir, manger, regarder, aller, faire, jouer*. So *going to go* is *aller aller*: *je vais aller au cinéma*.

**Negative**: *ne … pas* around **aller**: *je **ne** vais **pas** sortir, on **ne** va **pas** rester à la maison*.

**When**: *ce soir* (tonight), *demain* (tomorrow), *ce week-end*, *samedi prochain* (next Saturday), *la semaine prochaine* (next week), *après les cours* (after lessons), *pendant les vacances*.

steps.title: Où et quand ?
steps.body:
Plans need a **place** and a **time**.

**Places** with *à*: *au cinéma, au parc, au centre commercial* (shopping centre), *au stade, au restaurant, au café, à la piscine, à la patinoire* (ice rink), *à la plage, en ville* (into town), *chez moi / chez Léa* (at my house / at Léa's).

*À + le = au* — the rule from the sport topic — so *au cinéma*, never *à le cinéma*.

**Times**: *à sept heures, à sept heures et demie* (half past seven), *à huit heures moins le quart* (quarter to eight), *vers huit heures* (around eight). French timetables use the **24-hour clock**: *dix-neuf heures trente* is 19:30, or 7:30 pm. If the film lasts 2 hours it ends at 21h30.

**Meeting**: *on se retrouve devant le cinéma* (we'll meet in front of the cinema), *rendez-vous à huit heures* (meet at eight), *je passe te chercher* (I'll come and get you).

**Activities**: *voir un film* (see a film), *faire les magasins* (go shopping), *faire une promenade, manger au restaurant, aller à une fête* (go to a party), *faire du bowling*.

steps.title: Vouloir, pouvoir, devoir
steps.body:
Three verbs run the whole conversation, and all three take an **infinitive** — the same shape as the near future.

**Vouloir** (to want): *je veux, tu veux, il veut, nous voulons, vous voulez, ils veulent*. *Tu veux venir ?* — Do you want to come? *Je veux bien* — I'd like to (accepting).

**Pouvoir** (to be able): *je peux, tu peux, il peut, nous pouvons, vous pouvez, ils peuvent*. *Je ne peux pas* — I can't.

**Devoir** (to have to): *je dois, tu dois, il doit, nous devons, vous devez, ils doivent*. *Je dois rester à la maison* — I have to stay at home.

**Invitations**: *tu veux … ?*, *ça te dit de … ?* (do you fancy…?), *on va … ?*, *tu es libre samedi ?* (are you free on Saturday?).

**Accepting**: *oui, je veux bien*, *d'accord*, *bonne idée !*, *avec plaisir*.

**Refusing with a reason**: *désolé(e), je ne peux pas — je dois garder mon frère* (look after my brother), *je n'ai pas d'argent* (I have no money), *je suis fatigué(e)*, *mes parents ne veulent pas*.

**Then the plan**: *alors, on va … samedi prochain ?* — the near future closes the exchange.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Write the six forms of *aller*.
2. Translate: *I am going to watch a film tonight.*
3. Write *next Saturday* and *next week*.

**Part B.**

4. Write where you are going to go and at what time, using *au / à la*.
5. Invite a friend with *tu veux* and accept with *je veux bien*.
6. Refuse an invitation with *je ne peux pas* and a reason with *je dois*.

**Part C.**

7. Write what you are **not** going to do this weekend.
8. Arrange a meeting place and time with *on se retrouve*.
9. Write a five-line dialogue: invitation, acceptance, time, meeting place, a second plan.

For question 9, every verb after *aller, vouloir, pouvoir, devoir* is an infinitive.

visuals.alt: A blank five-row table for the student to build a dialogue about going out

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Get aller right every time.** *Vais, vas, va, allons, allez, vont.* The near future is only as good as this verb.

**Never conjugate the second verb.** *Je vais sortir*, not *je vais sors*. The same applies after *vouloir, pouvoir* and *devoir* — one conjugated verb, then infinitives.

**Wrap the negative round aller.** *Je ne vais pas sortir.* And after the negative, *des* shrinks: *je ne vais pas acheter **de** billets*.

**Contract the place.** *Au cinéma, au parc, à la piscine, chez moi.* *Chez* + a person is how you say *at someone's house* — *chez Léa* — and it needs no article.

**Know both clocks.** Timetables, listings and announcements use the 24-hour clock, in writing and aloud (*à dix-neuf heures trente*); in conversation people also say *à sept heures et demie*. Knowing both is a reading, listening and speaking skill.

**Give a reason when you refuse.** *Je ne peux pas parce que je dois garder ma sœur.* A refusal with *devoir* + infinitive is two structures in one line.

**Add an opinion about the plan.** *Ça va être génial !* — *aller* + *être* is the near future of *c'est*, and it lets you look forward to something.

**Chain plans with d'abord, ensuite, après.** *D'abord on va faire les magasins, ensuite on va manger, et après on va voir un film.* Three near futures in sequence is a full paragraph.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Near future = aller + infinitive**: *je vais sortir*.
- **Aller**: *vais, vas, va, allons, allez, vont*.
- The second verb is always an **infinitive**.
- Negative: *je **ne** vais **pas** sortir*.
- Time markers: *ce soir, demain, ce week-end, samedi prochain, la semaine prochaine*.
- Places: *au cinéma, à la piscine, en ville, chez moi*.
- Times: *à sept heures et demie*; 24-hour *dix-neuf heures trente* = 7:30 pm.
- Invite: *tu veux … ?, ça te dit de … ?, on va … ?*
- Accept: *oui, je veux bien, d'accord, bonne idée*.
- Refuse: *désolé(e), je ne peux pas, je dois …*
- **Vouloir, pouvoir, devoir** + infinitive.
- Meet: *on se retrouve devant … à …*
- Sequence: *d'abord, ensuite, après*.
- *Ça va être génial !*

examTechnique.body:
The near future is **aller + infinitive**: conjugate *aller*, leave the second verb alone, and wrap *ne … pas* round *aller*. Start with a time marker, add a place with *au / à la / chez* and a time.

In a dialogue, invite with *tu veux … ?*, accept with *je veux bien*, refuse with *je ne peux pas, je dois …*, and arrange with *on se retrouve devant … à …*.
examinerErrors: Writing je va instead of je vais.
Putting ne … pas round the infinitive.
Using à la maison de instead of chez.
Conjugating the verb after vouloir, pouvoir or devoir.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer conjugates **aller** faultlessly in several persons and never touches the infinitive, wraps the negative round *aller* and shrinks *des* to *de* after it. It places every plan with *au / à la / chez* and a time in both clock systems, chains plans with *d'abord, ensuite, après*, and runs a full invitation — *tu veux…?*, *je veux bien*, *désolé, je ne peux pas, je dois…* — with a reason. It looks forward with *ça va être génial*.
